source_text: Quid est enim malum, id est, peccatum? Voluntas sequendi quod iustitia vetat, et unde liberum est abstinere. Quid est ipsa voluntas? Motus animi, cogente nullo. Si ergo peccatum ex voluntate natum est, voluntas ex motu animi cogente nullo; nec nihili, nec tenebrarum conditio fecit ut esset hic motus, qui ideo a nullo cogitur, ut possit esse cogente nullo. Ac per hoc nullum est naturale, nullum originale peccatum: quia haec duo nomina unum indicant, id est, peccatum esse non voluntarium; praescripsit autem veritas, nisi voluntarium non posse esse peccatum; et ideo qui dicit malum esse quod constat ingenitum, non convincit in natura esse peccatum; sed se ostendit per pravitatem iudicii criminosum. Ecce responsum est, ad quod tu responderi non posse credebas. Oxymora prorsus fuit quaestio, quam tu arbitraris invictam.
pass_a_gloss: For what is evil, that is, sin? A will of following what justice forbids, and from which it is free to abstain. What is will itself? A motion of the mind, no one compelling. If therefore sin was born from will, will from a motion of the mind no one compelling; neither the condition of nothing, nor of darkness, made that this motion be, which therefore is compelled by no one, that it can be with no one compelling. And through this there is no natural, no original sin: because these two names indicate one thing, that is, that sin is not voluntary; but truth has prescribed that there cannot be sin except voluntary; and therefore he who says there is an evil which stands as inborn does not convict that there is sin in nature; but he shows himself criminal through a crookedness of judgment. Behold it has been replied, to which you believed it could not be replied. The question was altogether an oxymoron, which you judge unconquered.

lemmas.lexica: Blaise originalis; Julian's mali originalis, not a later system slogan
LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS liber=free; Blaise unde liberum est abstinere
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself

pass_b_english: For what is evil, that is, sin? The will to pursue what justice forbids and from which one is free to abstain. What is will itself? A movement of the mind under no compulsion. If sin therefore arose from will, and will from a movement of the mind under no compulsion, neither the condition of nothing nor that of darkness caused this movement to exist. It is compelled by no one precisely so that it can exist under no compulsion. Consequently, there is no natural sin and no original sin. These two names indicate one thing: sin that is not voluntary. But truth has ruled that sin cannot exist unless voluntary. Therefore whoever calls evil what is admittedly innate does not prove that sin exists in nature; he shows himself guilty through a perverse judgment. Here is the answer to what you thought could not be answered. The question you regard as invincible was altogether clever foolishness.

choices.why: Julian names the opinion of original evil (mali originalis) as what Rom 5:12's 'one man' crushed; keep his phrase, not a later original-sin system.
rejected: original sin (later system as default gloss)

choices.why: Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Freedom to abstain is required for will and sin.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
